implement-queue-using-stacks.pattern: Two stacks: an input stack and an output stack, transferring lazily (amortised O(1))

approaches.name: Keep the front on top by re-stacking on every push
approaches.idea: Keep one stack whose top is always the queue's front. To push, move everything to a helper stack, push the new value, and move everything back.
steps: `push(x)`: pop all of `s` onto `tmp`, push `x` onto `s`, then pop all of `tmp` back onto `s`.
`pop` / `peek`: the top of `s`. `empty`: whether `s` is empty.
approaches.why: push is O(n) every time (pop, peek and empty are O(1)).

approaches.name: Input and output stacks with lazy transfer
approaches.idea: Push onto `in`. Pop and peek from `out`; only when `out` is empty, pour all of `in` into it, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top.
steps: `push(x)`: push onto `in`.
`pop` / `peek`: if `out` is empty, move everything from `in` to `out`; then pop / read the top of `out`.
`empty`: both stacks are empty.
approaches.why: Amortised O(1) per operation: each element is pushed and popped at most twice in total. A single pop can cost O(n) when a transfer happens.

design-hashmap.pattern: Hashing with separate chaining (an array of buckets)

approaches.name: List of key–value pairs
approaches.idea: Keep all pairs in one list and search it linearly for every operation.
steps: `put`: find the key and update it, or append a new pair.
`get` / `remove`: scan for the key.
approaches.why: Every operation may scan all n stored pairs.

approaches.name: Direct addressing
approaches.idea: Keys are at most 10⁶, so use an array indexed by the key itself, with −1 meaning "absent".
steps: Allocate `table[0..10⁶]` filled with −1.
`put`: `table[key] = value`; `get`: `table[key]`; `remove`: `table[key] = −1`.
approaches.why: Every operation is one array access, but memory is proportional to the key universe U = 10⁶ even if only a handful of keys are stored — and impossible for large key spaces.

approaches.name: Buckets with separate chaining
approaches.idea: Hash each key to one of B buckets (`key % B`, B a prime) and keep a short list of pairs in each bucket. Keys that collide simply share a bucket.
steps: B = 10007 buckets, each a list of `(key, value)` pairs (created lazily).
`put`: in bucket `key % B`, update the key if found, else append.
`get` / `remove`: search only that bucket.
approaches.why: Average O(1 + n/B) per operation — about 10 entries per bucket at the maximum 10⁵ keys. Real hash tables also grow B as n grows to keep this constant.

min-stack.pattern: Store the running minimum alongside each element

approaches.name: Scan for the minimum
approaches.idea: Use an ordinary stack; `getMin` looks through every element.
steps: `push`, `pop`, `top` work on a plain array-backed stack.
`getMin` scans all elements and returns the smallest.
approaches.why: getMin is O(n), breaking the O(1) requirement (the other operations are O(1)).

approaches.name: Stack of (value, minimum so far) pairs
approaches.idea: When pushing, also record the minimum of the stack including this element. Popping then automatically restores the previous minimum, which is stored in the element below.
steps: `push(val)`: push `(val, min(val, current min))` (just `val` if the stack is empty).
`pop`: pop the pair. `top`: first field of the top pair.
`getMin`: second field of the top pair.
approaches.why: Every operation touches only the top. (A second stack that only stores new minimums saves memory when the minimum rarely changes.)

lru-cache.pattern: Hash map + doubly linked list (recency order)

approaches.name: List ordered by recency
approaches.idea: Keep `(key, value)` pairs in a list from least to most recently used. Every access finds the key by scanning and moves it to the end; eviction removes the first element.
steps: `get`: scan for the key; if found, move it to the end and return its value.
`put`: if the key exists, update and move it to the end; otherwise, if full, remove the first pair, then append.
approaches.why: Each operation scans and shifts up to `capacity` elements.

approaches.name: Hash map + doubly linked list
approaches.idea: A doubly linked list keeps the recency order (most recent next to the head) and can unlink any node in O(1); a hash map from key to node finds that node in O(1). Sentinel head and tail nodes remove edge cases.
steps: `get`: look up the node; if present, unlink it, re-insert it after `head`, and return its value.
`put`: if the key exists, update its value and move it to the front.
Otherwise create a node at the front and map it; if the size now exceeds `capacity`, unlink the node before `tail` and delete its key from the map.
approaches.why: Every step is a constant number of map and pointer operations. Built-ins package exactly this structure: Java's `LinkedHashMap` (access order), Python's `OrderedDict`, and a JavaScript `Map` (delete + re-set to move a key to the end).

insert-delete-getrandom-o1.pattern: Array for O(1) random access + hash map of value → index; delete by swapping with the last element

approaches.name: Array only
approaches.idea: Store the values in a dynamic array. Membership checks and removals search the array; random picks a uniform index.
steps: `insert`: if the value is not already in the array (linear search), append it.
`remove`: find it, delete it from the array.
`getRandom`: return the element at a uniformly random index.
approaches.why: insert and remove are O(n) because of the search (and the shift when deleting from the middle); getRandom is O(1).

approaches.name: Array + index map, swap-with-last removal
approaches.idea: The array gives O(1) uniform random picks; a hash map from value to its array index gives O(1) lookups. To delete from the middle in O(1), move the last element into the hole and pop the end.
steps: `insert`: if absent, record `index[val] = size` and append.
`remove`: if present, let `i = index[val]` and `last` be the final element; put `last` at `i`, set `index[last] = i`, pop the end, delete `val` from the map.
`getRandom`: element at a uniformly random index.
approaches.why: Average O(1) for all three: hash operations plus work at the array's end only. The array order changes on removal, which is fine for a set.

time-based-key-value-store.pattern: Hash map of key → timestamps in increasing order, binary search for the floor

approaches.name: Scan versions backwards
approaches.idea: For each key keep its versions in the order they were set (timestamps increase). `get` walks backwards from the newest version until it finds a timestamp ≤ the query.
steps: `set`: append `(timestamp, value)` to the key's list.
`get`: walk the list from the end; return the first value whose timestamp ≤ `timestamp`, else "".
approaches.why: `set` is O(1), but `get` can scan all n versions of a key.

approaches.name: Binary search for the last timestamp ≤ t
approaches.idea: Because each key's timestamps arrive in increasing order, its list is already sorted. Binary-search for the last timestamp that is ≤ the query.
steps: `set`: append the timestamp and the value to the key's parallel lists.
`get`: binary-search the first timestamp > `timestamp`; the answer is the element just before it, or "" if there is none.
approaches.why: `set` is O(1) (amortised) and `get` is O(log n) per key. A `TreeMap.floorEntry` per key would also work, at O(log n) for both.

peeking-iterator.pattern: Iterator wrapper with a one-element lookahead cache

approaches.name: Copy everything up front
approaches.idea: Drain the underlying iterator into a list in the constructor, then serve `peek`, `next` and `hasNext` from the list with an index.
steps: Constructor: read every element into `items`; `pos = 0`.
`peek`: `items[pos]`; `next`: `items[pos++]`; `hasNext`: `pos < items.length`.
approaches.why: O(n) up front and O(n) memory — it defeats the purpose of an iterator, which may be huge or infinite.

approaches.name: Cache exactly one element ahead
approaches.idea: Always hold the next element (if any) in a field. `peek` returns it; `next` returns it and refills the cache from the underlying iterator.
steps: Constructor: `has = it.hasNext()`; if so, `cached = it.next()`.
`peek`: return `cached`. `hasNext`: return `has`.
`next`: remember `cached`, refill (`has = it.hasNext()`, `cached = it.next()` if so), return the remembered value.
approaches.why: Each call does at most one call on the underlying iterator and keeps one extra element.

flatten-nested-list-iterator.pattern: Lazy DFS with an explicit stack of (list, position) frames

approaches.name: Flatten everything in the constructor
approaches.idea: Recursively walk the whole nested structure once, collecting integers into a flat list; then iterate over that list.
steps: Constructor: DFS over `nestedList`, appending each integer in order.
`next`: return `flat[pos++]`; `hasNext`: `pos < flat.length`.
approaches.why: N integers and L lists are all visited up front, and the whole flat copy is kept (D = nesting depth for the recursion). Fine here, but it does all the work even if the caller stops early.

approaches.name: Lazy stack of positions
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of frames `(list, index)` — the DFS call stack, made explicit. `hasNext` advances until the top frame points at an integer, descending into sub-lists and popping finished ones. `next` then just returns that integer.
steps: Start with one frame for `nestedList` at index 0.
`hasNext`: while the stack is not empty — if the top frame is finished, pop it; if it points at an integer, return true; if it points at a list, step past it and push a frame for that list.
Return false when the stack empties (this also skips empty lists like `[[]]`).
`next`: call `hasNext`, then return the integer at the top frame and advance it.
approaches.why: Amortised O(1) per call: each list and integer is stepped over once across the whole iteration. Only the current path (depth D) is stored, and nothing is copied.

snapshot-array.pattern: Per-index version history + binary search (store only changes, not copies)

approaches.name: Copy the whole array on every snap
approaches.idea: Keep the current array; `snap` saves a full copy. `get` reads from the saved copy.
steps: `set`: write into the current array.
`snap`: append a copy of the current array; return its index.
`get(i, id)`: `snapshots[id][i]`.
approaches.why: `set` and `get` are O(1), but each snap copies `length` values — up to 5·10⁴ × 10⁵ operations and memory in the worst case.

approaches.name: Per-index change log + binary search
approaches.idea: For each index, record only the changes as `(snapId, value)` pairs, where `snapId` is the snapshot the change will belong to. A `get` finds the last change with `snapId ≤ id` by binary search.
steps: `set(i, v)`: if the last entry of `history[i]` has the current snap id, overwrite its value; otherwise append `(snapCount, v)`.
`snap()`: return `snapCount++` — nothing is copied.
`get(i, id)`: binary-search `history[i]` for the last entry with `snapId ≤ id`; return its value, or 0 if there is none.
approaches.why: `set` and `snap` are O(1), `get` is O(log s) for s recorded changes at that index; memory grows only with the number of `set` calls.

design-twitter.pattern: Per-user tweet lists + k-way merge with a max-heap (merge k sorted lists)

approaches.name: Scan the global timeline
approaches.idea: Keep every tweet in one list in posting order. For a feed, walk it from the newest end and keep tweets by the user or anyone they follow, stopping at 10.
steps: `postTweet`: append `(userId, tweetId)` to the global list.
`follow` / `unfollow`: add to / remove from the user's followee set.
`getNewsFeed`: scan backwards, collecting tweets whose author is the user or a followee, until 10 are found.
approaches.why: A feed may scan all T tweets ever posted if the user's network is quiet; the other operations are O(1).

approaches.name: Per-user lists merged with a max-heap
approaches.idea: Each user's tweets form a list already sorted by time. A feed is the top 10 of a k-way merge of the user's list and their followees' lists: put each list's newest tweet in a max-heap by time, pop the newest, and push the next-older tweet from the same list.
steps: `postTweet`: append `(time++, tweetId)` to the user's own list.
`getNewsFeed`: for the user and each followee with tweets, push their newest `(time, tweetId, user, index)`.
Pop up to 10 times; after each pop, push that user's previous tweet if there is one.
approaches.why: Building the heap costs O(F) for F followees, and only 10 pops follow — independent of how many tweets exist overall.

lfu-cache.pattern: Hash map + frequency buckets (each an LRU-ordered list) + a min-frequency pointer

approaches.name: Scan for the victim
approaches.idea: Store each key with its value, use count and the time it was last used. On eviction, scan all keys for the smallest `(count, lastUsed)`.
steps: `get`: if present, increment its count, stamp the current time, return the value.
`put` on an existing key: update the value and touch it the same way.
`put` of a new key when full: remove the key with the smallest count, breaking ties by the oldest time; then insert with count 1.
approaches.why: `get` is O(1), but every eviction scans all stored keys.

approaches.name: Frequency buckets with LRU order and minFreq
approaches.idea: Group keys by use count. Each bucket keeps its keys in recency order (an insertion-ordered set or linked list), so the eviction victim is the oldest key in the lowest non-empty bucket. Track that lowest count in `minFreq`.
steps: `touch(key)`: move the key from bucket `f` to the back of bucket `f + 1`; if bucket `f` became empty and `f == minFreq`, increment `minFreq`.
`get`: if present, `touch` it and return the value.
`put` on an existing key: update the value and `touch` it.
`put` of a new key: if full, remove the first key of bucket `minFreq`; insert the new key into bucket 1 and set `minFreq = 1`.
approaches.why: Every step is a constant number of hash-map and linked-list operations. `minFreq` only ever increases by one during a touch, or resets to 1 on insertion, so it never needs a search.

code.python:
class LFUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.min_freq = 0
        self.entries = {}  # key -> [value, count]
        self.buckets = defaultdict(OrderedDict)  # count -> keys, oldest first

    def _touch(self, key, e):
        bucket = self.buckets[e[1]]
        del bucket[key]
        if not bucket and self.min_freq == e[1]:
            self.min_freq += 1
        e[1] += 1
        self.buckets[e[1]][key] = None

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        e = self.entries.get(key)
        if e is None:
            return -1
        self._touch(key, e)
        return e[0]

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.entries:
            e = self.entries[key]
            e[0] = value
            self._touch(key, e)
            return
        if len(self.entries) == self.capacity:
            victim, _ = self.buckets[self.min_freq].popitem(last=False)
            del self.entries[victim]
        self.entries[key] = [value, 1]
        self.buckets[1][key] = None
        self.min_freq = 1

insert-delete-getrandom-o1-duplicates-al.pattern: Array + hash map of value → set of indices; delete by swapping with the last element

approaches.name: Array only
approaches.idea: Keep every copy in a dynamic array. A uniformly random index automatically weights each value by its number of copies.
steps: `insert`: note whether the value is already present (linear search), then append.
`remove`: find one copy and delete it.
`getRandom`: element at a uniformly random index.
approaches.why: insert and remove search (and shift) the array; getRandom is O(1).

approaches.name: Array + map of value → set of positions
approaches.idea: Like the no-duplicates version, but each value maps to the set of all positions holding a copy. To remove one copy, take any of its positions, move the last element into it, and fix both values' position sets.
steps: `insert`: add `size` to `pos[val]`, append `val`; return whether the set was empty before.
`remove`: if `pos[val]` is empty, return false. Take any `i` from it; let `last = values[n − 1]`.
Set `values[i] = last`; add `i` to `pos[last]` and remove `n − 1` from it (in that order, which also works when `last == val` or `i == n − 1`); pop the end.
`getRandom`: element at a uniformly random index.
approaches.why: Average O(1): a constant number of hash-set operations plus work at the array end. The array holds each copy once, so random indices are weighted by copy count.
